info.bio:
De origen netamente irlandés y representado por la impagable imagen de Shane MacGowan, su cantante y lider, The Pogues conjugan aires populares, voluntad épica y reflexiones de caracter social con una grosería altisonante que a fuerza de altercados acabó por identificarles.
     
Desde una plataforma folk, pero con planteamientos punk, el septeto The Pogues encabeza una corriente que hace música de tradición gaélica con intensidad y arrojo

scenes.name: Indie, C86 y el giro retro
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: En 1985 la energía se ha disipado: el new pop cae en la decadencia (Live Aid, «una tragedia para el pop»), los singles independientes venden la mitad que en 1980 y «independiente» se convierte en «indie», un género de guitarras sucias, voces pálidas y nostalgia de los sesenta, oposición impotente al mainstream. El futurismo da paso al «rock de coleccionista»: The Jesus and Mary Chain (Psychocandy: Ronettes y Beach Boys con feedback), el sello Creation y Primal Scream, la cassette C86 de NME (The Pastels, Shop Assistants, The Soup Dragons, June Brides) y su culto a la inocencia, que reaparecerá en el riot grrrl. The Smiths y R.E.M., contra los ochenta; Hüsker Dü, Sonic Youth, Butthole Surfers y Dinosaur Jr. redescubren el acid rock; de ahí, Nirvana.

scenes.name: Cruces del punk: de Fugazi al punk-pop
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: A finales de los ochenta el punk es el más vivo de los subgéneros del rock: miles de bandas ensayando en garajes, un lenguaje universal como no se veía desde los sesenta. Nueva York: Adrenalin O.D., el straight-edge de Youth Of Today y Gorilla Biscuits, el crossover punk-metal (Cro-Mags, Prong, Danzig). Washington lanza a Pussy Galore (la irrelevancia hecha relevante), Unrest y Fugazi de Ian MacKaye, que abstrae el hardcore en una forma teatral de compromiso ético y estético (Repeater, Steady Diet Of Nothing, Red Medicine), y Royal Trux (Twin Infinitives, «un Trout Mask Replica para la generación grunge»). El punk-pop de Mr T Experience, Dwarves, Henry Rollins, L7 (pioneras del «foxcore»), Lemonheads, Screeching Weasel, Goo Goo Dolls, Fastbacks, Shonen Knife; el «rogue folk» de los Pogues, Membranes y Chumbawamba.

podcast.title: Shane McGowan's Firing (1991)
podcast.body: The Pogues fired their original singer, Shane McGowan, in 1991 due to his excessive drinking. Joe Strummer was subsequently asked to fill his position. "In 1991, they fired their singer Shane McGowan for being a drunk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pelvis Fracture and Pneumonia (2015)
podcast.body: In the summer of 2015, Shane MacGowan fell and broke his pelvis while leaving his Dublin home for a recording studio, an injury that thereafter required him to use a wheelchair and led to a serious case of pneumonia, hospitalizing him. "In the summer of 2015, as he was leaving home in Dublin for a date at a recording studio, he fell and broke his pelvis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Viral Encephalitis Diagnosis (2022)
podcast.body: In December 2022, Shane MacGowan's health deteriorated further when he was diagnosed with viral encephalitis, leading to another hospitalization. "Things got worse in December 2022 when he was diagnosed with viral encephalitis."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Dublin Funeral Procession (2023)
podcast.body: On December 8, 2023, Shane MacGowan's coffin was paraded through the streets of Dublin in a horse-drawn carriage on its way to his funeral, with thousands of mourners, including the President of Ireland, attending to bid farewell. "On December 8, 2023, his coffin was paraded through the streets of Dublin on a horse-drawn carriage to the funeral."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Repeated Hospitalizations (2023)
podcast.body: In July 2023, Shane MacGowan was admitted to the hospital again with a new infection, remaining there for four months before doctors determined they could no longer help him. "He was back in the hospital eight months later in July 2023 with a new infection."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Cait O'Riordan's Departure
podcast.body: Cait O'Riordan, the Pogues' bass player for whom the female part of "Fairy Tale of New York" was originally written, left the band after she "had run off with Elvis Castell." This departure forced the song to be shelved for Christmas 1986. "It had been written for Cater Reardon, a Pogs bass player, but she had run off with Elvis Castell, so that shelled the song for Christmas 1986."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chris Berkett's Work
podcast.body: Chris Berkett worked on records for The Pogues, which sold tens of millions of copies. "talking heads, the poges, Shunato Connor, Bob Geldoff, Quincy Jones, Buffy St. Marie, Sting Peter Gabriel and many others."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Chronic Health Issues
podcast.body: Shane MacGowan suffered from stomach ulcers and alcoholic hepatitis, and nearly all of his teeth rotted and fell out due to his lifestyle. "There were stomach ulcers and a case of alcoholic hepatitis. Almost all of his teeth rotted and fell out."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Collaboration with Steve Lillywhite
podcast.body: The Pogues have worked with Steve Lillywhite, a very famous record producer. "He's also worked with Morrissey and The Pogues."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Continued Falls and Injuries
podcast.body: Despite dental improvements, Shane MacGowan's falls persisted; in February 2021, he tripped at home and broke a knee, confining him to bed. "In February 2021, he tripped at his home and broke a knee that laid him up in bed."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Creators of Celtic Punk
podcast.body: The Pogues are widely credited with creating the entire genre of Celtic punk. "In fact, I'd go as far as to say that they created the whole genre of Celtic punk."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Death from Pneumonia
podcast.body: A week after his discharge, a priest was called to Shane MacGowan's home, and he died from pneumonia later that day, with his wife Victoria by his side. "Shane McGowan died from pneumonia later that day with his wife, Victoria, next to him."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Detox and Temporary Sobriety
podcast.body: The hospitalization resulting from his fractured pelvis and pneumonia prompted Shane MacGowan to finally detox and become sober for a period, although he would eventually relapse. "It was then that he finally detoxed and became sober for a while, anyway, because he would eventually relapse."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Difficult Live Introduction
podcast.body: The speaker recounted a challenging experience trying to introduce The Pogues, specifically Shane MacGowan. He couldn't be found initially because he was out drinking. When located, he was hustled onto the stage to sing before he passed out, preventing the speaker from making the introduction. The speaker could smell MacGowan from 15 feet away, but noted that he still "knew all the words" once he got to the microphone. "I never got to introduce the band because they wanted to get Shane in front of a mic as quickly as they possibly could. I got to within 15 feet of him and I could smell him. I really could."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Discharge from St. Vincent's Hospital
podcast.body: Shane MacGowan was discharged from St. Vincent's Hospital in Dublin on November 23, 2023, as medical professionals could no longer provide further assistance. "Shane was discharged from St. Vincent's hospital in Dublin on November 23, 2023."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Drug Habits and Physical Trauma
podcast.body: Shane MacGowan's drug use included LSD and a developed heroin habit, which, combined with heavy drinking, led to frequent falls, collisions, fights, and occasional car accidents. "He liked LSD and developed a heroin habit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Alcohol Introduction
podcast.body: Shane MacGowan began drinking at the age of five, with his parents offering him "a bit of Guinness to help the lad sleep," which developed into heavy drinking by his teenage years. "Shane began drinking when he was five, thanks to his parents."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Material Produced by Elvis Costello
podcast.body: Elvis Costello helped produce some of the early material for The Pogues, lending his production expertise to the band. His involvement highlights his supportive role within the music community, particularly for emerging artists. "Just ask any fan of the poges how Elvis helped produce some of their early material."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Elvis Costello

podcast.title: Extensive Dental Procedure
podcast.body: Following his period of sobriety, Shane MacGowan underwent a significant dental procedure to fix his mouth, involving the installation of a brand new set of teeth using eight titanium implants over a nine-hour operation, which was documented in a TV show. "First, though, he had his mouth fixed. A brand new set of teeth was installed using eight titanium implants in a procedure that lasted nine hours."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Founding Partners and Previous Bands
podcast.body: Shane MacGowan and Spider Stacy met in the toilets at a Ramones show at the Roundhouse in London in 1977. Both had previously been members of several other bands, including The Nippley Rectors (later shortened to The Nipps), the Millwall Chain Saws, and the New Republicans, before forming The Pogues in 1982. "Shane's co-founding partner was Spider Stacy, a guy he met in the toilets at a Ramone show at the Roundhouse in London in 1977. Both had been in several bands with names like The Nippley Rectors, later shortened to just The Nipps, plus they were in the Millwall Chain Saws and the new Republicans."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Future Episode Plans
podcast.body: The speaker plans to create an episode on Shane MacGowan in the new year for 2024, highlighting The Pogues' significant role in integrating Irish Celtic folk tradition into punk rock. "I'm going to have to do something on Shane in the new year because the Pogs were so important when it comes to bringing that Irish Celtic folk tradition into punk rock and there's a great story there, a really great story."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: OGHONM 1000th Episode: The Q&A From the Live Recording

podcast.title: Members Acting in Straight to Hell
podcast.body: Members of The Pogues appeared in Alex Cox's 1987 movie *Straight to Hell*, a "very, very weird western" that also featured Joe Strummer and Courtney Love. This collaboration highlights the cross-pollination of musicians and artists in independent film projects during the late 1980s.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Origin of Name and Location
podcast.body: The band was originally named Pogue Mahone, a Gaelic phrase roughly translating to "Kiss My Ass," which they had to shorten to The Pogues due to complaints when they received early radio airplay on the BBC. Despite their strong Irish identity, the band was actually formed in the King's Cross area of London. "Their original name was Pogue Mahone, which in a rough translation is galec for Kiss My Ass. They had to shorten that because when they got some early radio airplane on the BBC, they got a bunch of complaints. And while they were proud of being from Ireland, they were actually formed in the King's Cross area of London."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shane MacGowan's Early Punk Anecdote
podcast.body: Co-founder Shane MacGowan, a devoted hardcore punk fan, famously had part of his ear bitten off during a Clash show in 1976. A newspaper photo the following day captured Shane holding his ear in front of the stage with Joe Strummer towering above him, accompanied by the headline "Cannibalism at Clash Gig." "They were founded by Shane McGowan, a hard-drinking hardcore punk fan, who once had part of his ear bitten off during a clash show in 1976. The newspaper, the next day carried a photo of Shane holding his right ear in front of the stage with Joe Strummer towering above him, and the headline read Cannibalism at Clash Gig."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shane MacGowan's Funeral
podcast.body: Following Shane MacGowan's death in Dublin on November 30, 2023, he received a massive public sendoff, with people lining the streets to pay their respects to his funeral procession. "When Shane died in Dublin on November 30, 2023, he was given a massive sendoff as people line the streets to give the respects to the funeral procession."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shane MacGowan's Lifelong Unhealthy Lifestyle
podcast.body: Shane MacGowan was never a healthy man, leading a life marked by heavy drinking, drug use, and self-inflicted bodily trauma, making his survival to age 65 seem like a "miracle." "Now he was never a healthy man. So the fact that he lived to 65 is pretty much a miracle."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Sid Vicious's Pogo Origin Story
podcast.body: Shane McGowan, the singer of The Pogs and a big punk fan, offered an alternative explanation for Sid Vicious's Pogo dance. He suggested that Sid's dance style was a result of him wearing a tight leather poncho that restricted his movements, forcing him to simply jump up and down. "He says Sid's dance was the result of him insisting on wearing a tight leather poncho that restricted his dance movements to just jumping up and down."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Steve Lillywhite's Role
podcast.body: Producer Steve Lillywhite, known for his work on U2's first three albums, played a crucial role in the development of "Fairy Tale of New York." He produced The Pogues' third album, "If I Should Fall From Grace With God," and, being married to Kirsty MacColl, arranged for her to record the female vocal parts. "The producer was a guy named Steve Lillie White. He had helped you too with their first three albums."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Tumultuous Career and Split
podcast.body: The Pogues had a critically acclaimed but highly tumultuous career. Shane MacGowan was at one point kicked out of the band and temporarily replaced by Joe Strummer, only to be welcomed back later. The band experienced breakups and long hiatuses, ultimately splitting permanently in 2014 when Shane MacGowan's struggles with drinking and drug problems became unmanageable. "The pokes would go on to have a critically acclaimed but tumultuous career, which would see Shane kicked out replaced by Joe Strummer of all people. And then welcome back in. They were breakups, long hiatus and finally a permanent split in 2014 when Shane could no longer outrun his drinking and drug problems."
